context_question: What are the primary outcomes Tarrant County wants this integrated justice capability to achieve for indigent defense services, and how will success be measured?
answer:
The main outcome is to make appointed-counsel processing faster, more consistent, and less manual so the Office of Attorney Appointments can handle requests with better information and fewer delays. We also want smoother coordination across the criminal justice community, with timely notifications and better sharing of defendant and case details so appointments are made accurately.
Success would probably be measured by reduced turnaround time from request to appointment, fewer data entry errors or missing information, and fewer follow-up calls or emails to chase down case details. We’d also look at whether users can see the status of a request more easily and whether notifications are getting the right people at the right time, but the exact metrics would still need to be defined with the team.

context_question: Which stakeholder groups or user roles will interact with this integrated justice capability, and what responsibilities or permissions should each role have?
answer:
The main users will be staff in the Office of Attorney Appointments, since they’ll be receiving and processing the requests and coordinating the appointment workflow. We’ll also have judges or court staff submitting or initiating requests, and attorneys who may need appointment information and notifications. On the justice-system side, there will likely be jail, clerk, prosecutor, and maybe public defender or other court-connected staff who provide or consume case information, though the exact role permissions still need to be worked out.
In general, Office staff should be able to review cases, verify eligibility information, assign or route appointments, and send notifications. Court users should probably be able to create or submit requests and see status updates relevant to their cases, while attorneys should receive appointment details and updates but not edit case records. Other agencies would likely have more limited access, mostly to share or view the specific information they’re responsible for.

context_question: What are the key business rules that should govern how appointed-counsel requests are reviewed, prioritized, approved or rejected, assigned to attorneys, and routed for notifications—for example, eligibility checks, exceptions, deadlines, or criteria that determine who can act on a request and when?
answer:
A request should not move forward until the core defendant and case information is complete enough to make a decision, and the office needs to be able to verify that the person actually qualifies for appointed counsel under county rules. If something is missing or the case is in an exception category, staff should be able to hold it, reject it, or route it for manual review instead of forcing an automatic approval.
Priority would usually depend on case type, court requirements, and any deadlines already attached to the matter, so urgent hearings or expiring timelines should surface first. Only authorized Office of Attorney Appointments staff should approve or assign counsel, while courts may initiate requests and other agencies may provide supporting information but not make the appointment decision. Notifications should go out when a request is received, when it is approved or rejected, when counsel is assigned, and when something changes that affects the parties involved, but I’d want to verify the exact trigger points and exception handling with the team.

context_question: What specific types of requests or case situations should be treated as exception categories, and for each one, what should the system do—such as hold, reject, or route to manual review?
answer:
The most obvious exceptions would be requests with missing identity or case details, duplicate requests, conflicts of interest, or situations where the person is clearly not eligible based on the information available. Those should usually be held or routed to manual review rather than automatically approved, because staff need a chance to verify what’s wrong and correct it if possible.
We’d also treat special case types, like emergencies, late-night or same-day requests, and maybe cases involving minors, detention status changes, or unusual court orders, as manual-review items if they don’t fit the normal workflow. If the issue is a hard disqualifier, then rejection makes sense; if it’s just incomplete or ambiguous, holding the request and sending it to the right staff is better. The exact exception list and action for each one would still need to be defined with the office and the courts.

context_question: Can you describe how approval authority should be structured for appointed-counsel requests—for example, which specific roles or levels within the Office of Attorney Appointments can approve, assign, override, or manually review requests, and whether any approval rules vary by case type, court, urgency, or exception category?
answer:
In general, I’d expect frontline appointment staff to handle intake, review completeness, and prepare the request, but not necessarily have authority to override a rule or make a final exception decision on their own. Supervisors or designated lead staff should probably be the ones who can approve exceptions, override routing, or manually assign counsel when the normal workflow doesn’t fit.
I would expect some approval rules to vary by case type and urgency, especially for emergency appointments or special categories that need faster handling. Court-specific rules may also matter if a particular court requires certain review steps before assignment, and any exception category that touches eligibility or conflicts should likely require higher-level review. The exact approval matrix isn’t fully defined yet, so we’d need to confirm which roles get which permissions and where the cutoff points are.

context_question: For the agencies that will share or consume case information, what data-sharing rules should govern what each agency can see, provide, or update—for example, should access vary by agency type, case type, specific field, or record status, and are there any information-sharing restrictions or approval steps we need to account for?
answer:
Yes, access will definitely need to vary by agency type, and in some cases by case type or by the status of the record. For example, a court or clerk user might need broader visibility into case and appointment status, while a jail or prosecutor user should only see the fields they need to support the process, and updates should be limited to the information that agency is responsible for.
We also need to account for restricted data, like confidential defendant information, sealed matters, or notes that are only visible to office staff or supervisors. Some updates may need approval or validation before they become part of the official record, especially if they affect eligibility, counsel assignment, or court deadlines. I don’t know yet whether there are formal county data-sharing agreements or statutory restrictions that will drive the final rules, so that would need to be confirmed.

context_question: Could you share more about specific challenges or priorities you expect during the migration process to ensure a smooth transition without disrupting ongoing operations? For example, are there particular data issues, workflow handoffs, or user readiness concerns you want to address?
answer: The biggest concern is data quality, especially duplicate records, missing fields, and inconsistent case identifiers across systems. Workflow handoffs are also tricky because staff will need a clear point where old processes stop and the new one takes over, with no gaps in active cases. User readiness matters too, so training and a short support period after go-live would be important to keep people from falling back to manual work.

context_question: You’ve highlighted important concerns about data quality and workflow handoffs. To build on that, how do you envision the actual migration approach? For example, would you prefer a phased rollout where parts of the system or certain case types move over gradually, or a big switch all at once? Also, what kind of fallback or parallel operation plans would you want in place to ensure staff can keep working smoothly if any issues arise during the transition?
answer: I’d strongly prefer a phased rollout, probably starting with a limited set of case types or a single office area before expanding countywide. That gives us a chance to catch mapping or workflow issues without putting the whole operation at risk. We’d want a parallel run or fallback plan for a short period, so staff can verify records in both places or revert to the old process if something critical fails during go-live.

context_question: You’ve shared great insights on preferring a phased rollout and fallback plans. To help us plan better, could you describe any specific challenges or priorities you expect during the migration itself? For example, are there particular data issues, workflow handoffs, or user readiness concerns that you think will be critical to address to keep operations smooth throughout the transition?
answer: Data integrity is the biggest priority, especially making sure each defendant, case, and appointment ties back correctly across systems. We’d also need to be very careful with workflow handoffs so there’s no confusion about who is responsible for an appointment at any point during the transition. On the user side, the main challenge is getting staff comfortable enough with the new screens and process so they can work efficiently from day one.

context_question: You’ve shared valuable thoughts on AI-driven prioritization and the need for transparency. Building on that, are there any known or anticipated conflicts between requirements that might complicate designing the notification system? For example, how do you see balancing the risk of alert fatigue with the need to ensure urgent cases reliably get the attention they require?
answer: Yes, that balance is definitely a concern. We don’t want staff getting buried in too many routine alerts, but we also can’t afford to miss something urgent or time-sensitive. My sense is the system should use clear priority levels, suppress duplicates where possible, and let staff tune noncritical notifications without blocking the truly important ones.

context_question: You’ve given great insight on managing alert fatigue with priority levels and tuning. Are there any other known or anticipated conflicts between requirements—maybe around timing, user roles, or policy constraints—that you think might complicate designing or implementing the notification system effectively?
answer: Timing is one possible conflict, because some notifications need to be immediate while others are better batched or delayed to avoid interrupting staff during busy periods. User roles can also complicate things, since different people need different levels of detail and not everyone should see the same case information. Policy and confidentiality rules will be important too, because we have to make sure notifications share enough to be useful without exposing information to the wrong audience.

context_question: Thanks for highlighting those important conflicts around timing, roles, and confidentiality. To build on that, could you describe any operational or organizational constraints—like staffing patterns, shift changes, or policy rules—that might influence how notification prioritization and override features should be designed or deployed?
answer: Staffing patterns matter a lot because coverage isn’t always constant, so the system should account for evenings, weekends, and times when fewer people are available. We also have to respect policy rules about who can override a notification or reassign an urgent item, since that should not be open to everyone. In practice, I’d expect supervisors to have more flexibility, but with an audit trail so we can see who changed what and why.

context_question: Can you walk me through the main reasons your organization is looking to improve appointed-counsel administration and justice information sharing, and what business outcomes you most want that change to support?
answer:
Right now the main issue is that too much of the appointment process depends on manual steps, phone calls, and pulling information from different places, so it takes longer than it should to get counsel assigned and keep everyone informed. We also want to reduce errors and gaps in case information, because when defendant or case details are incomplete, it slows down appointments and creates extra work for staff and the courts.
The business outcomes we care about most are faster, more accurate attorney appointments, better visibility into case status for the people handling the requests, and more consistent communication across the justice partners involved. Ultimately, we want to improve service to indigent defendants, reduce administrative burden on the office, and make the process more reliable and trackable end to end.

context_question: What specific service outcome for indigent defense coordination is most important to you beyond improving administration and information sharing?
answer: The most important service outcome is making sure qualified counsel is appointed as quickly as possible when a request comes in, without delays caused by missing information or back-and-forth communication. We want defendants and the courts to have confidence that the process is timely, fair, and consistent every time.

context_question: Do you want to define any specific boundaries or exceptions for getting qualified counsel appointed quickly—for example, cases where key information is missing or the request needs review—or should we note that as still undecided for now?
answer: We should treat that as still somewhat undecided for now. In practice, if key information is missing or something doesn’t look right, the request would need review before an appointment is made, but the exact rules and exception handling still need to be worked out with our team.

context_question: When a request needs to be reviewed before an appointment can be made, how do you want that review to work in practice across the county justice partners involved, and what information or handoffs need to be part of that process?
answer:
In practice, the review should route to the right staff or partner based on what’s missing or what needs clarification, so the request doesn’t just sit in a queue. We need the ability to see the case details, defendant information, charge information, and any notes from the requesting court or agency, then send it back or forward it to the right place for correction or approval.
The handoff needs to include enough context so the next person knows exactly what needs attention, plus a status trail so everyone can see where the request is and who last touched it. If a court, jail, or other justice partner has to provide something before counsel can be appointed, that exchange should be captured in the system rather than handled only by phone or email.

context_question: When people in your community use terms like “case,” “charge,” “defendant,” “request for counsel,” or “appointment,” what do those words mean in practice, and are there any local variations or terms you use differently across courts, jails, and other partners?
answer:
In practice, a case is the overall criminal matter tied to the defendant, while a charge is each specific offense or count within that matter. A request for counsel is the formal ask to appoint an attorney for an eligible defendant, and an appointment is the actual assignment of that attorney to the case.
We do have some local variation in wording across courts and jails, mostly in how they refer to the same workflow step or document, but the core meaning is usually the same. The one thing I’d be careful about is that different partners may use their own shorthand, so the system should probably be flexible about labels while still storing the same underlying information consistently.

context_question: What local terms or labels do courts, jails, or other partners use for the defendant, respondent, and case identifiers, and are there any situations where those identifiers should be treated differently or mapped back to a standard value in the system?
answer:
The biggest variation is usually in how they refer to the person and the case number. Some partners will say defendant, some may use inmate or accused depending on the setting, and the case identifiers can vary by court, jail, or agency record number even when they’re talking about the same matter.
Yes, those identifiers definitely need to be mapped back to a standard value in the system where possible, because we’ll need one consistent way to find and track the request across partners. In some situations there may be multiple identifiers for the same person or case, so the system should keep the local reference too, but tie it to a single standard record for coordination and reporting.

context_question: Besides the Office of Attorney Appointments, who else needs to be able to request, review, appoint, or receive notifications for an appointment request?
answer:
Courts are the main outside group that would need to request or initiate a request, and jail staff may also need to provide information or confirm eligibility details. Depending on the workflow, judges or court staff may need to review or approve certain requests, and appointed attorneys obviously need to receive the assignment and related notices.
Other justice partners may need notifications too, but the exact list varies by case type and local workflow, so I’d want to confirm the complete set with the team.

context_question: You mentioned that courts are the main outside group; for appointment processing, do you want to name the primary user roles now, or should we treat that as still tentative until you confirm whether any other role should be considered primary?
answer: We should treat that as still tentative for now. I can say the likely primary roles are court staff, Office of Attorney Appointments staff, and appointed attorneys, but I’d rather confirm whether judges or jail staff need to be treated as primary users before we lock that down.

context_question: What typically triggers an appointed-counsel request today, and who or what initiates it?
answer: Most often it starts when a defendant is identified as needing counsel in a criminal case, usually through the court process or after an intake or custody event. The request may be initiated by court staff, and in some situations jail staff or another justice partner may provide the information that causes the request to be created.

context_question: About how many appointed-counsel requests come in during a typical day or week, and are there any predictable spikes or timing patterns you want to account for?
answer: I don’t have a reliable number offhand, and I’d want to verify that with the team before giving you anything precise. There are definitely patterns, though, like busier periods around court dockets and after weekends or holidays when requests can pile up.

context_question: When a request is in review, what should the status trail show about who owns it at each step, especially if it has to be sent back for missing information or handed off to another staff member or partner?
answer:
The status trail should show who currently owns the request, who last touched it, and when it moved from one step to the next. If it’s sent back for missing information, it should clearly show that it’s awaiting correction and from whom, so we can see whether it’s with the court, jail, or our office.
If it’s handed off to another staff member or partner, we need the history to preserve the full chain of custody, not just the current owner. That way anyone reviewing it later can understand where it stalled and who was responsible at each point.

context_question: When a request needs to be resubmitted or closed out, what business rules or handoff steps should govern that process, and what should happen if it can’t be completed right away?
answer:
If it needs resubmission, the system should keep the original request linked to the corrected version so we don’t lose the history. The person or office that identified the missing information should be able to send it back with a reason, and the request should stay open until the needed items are provided or the case is formally closed out.
If it can’t be completed right away, it should move into a pending or held state with a clear explanation of what’s blocking it and who is responsible for the next action. We’d also want alerts or reminders so it doesn’t sit there unnoticed.

context_question: What specific request intake fields are required before the Office of Attorney Appointments can evaluate a request for appointed counsel?
answer: At a minimum, we’d need the defendant’s identifying information, the case number, the charging or case type, and enough contact or location information to verify the person and follow up if needed. We’d also need the request date, the requesting court or agency, and any indigency information that’s available at intake. If some of that is missing, the request can still be created, but it can’t really be evaluated until the key items are filled in.

context_question: Which external parties besides the requesting court should receive notices or updates for an appointed-counsel request, and under what case types or workflow conditions would each recipient be included?
answer:
Besides the requesting court, we’d usually need to notify the defendant, the appointed attorney once assigned, and sometimes jail staff if the person is in custody and the update affects transport or appearance. In some cases, the prosecutor or another justice partner may need a notice if the appointment changes a hearing timeline or there’s a workflow step that affects the case schedule.
Who gets included depends on the case type and where the request is in the process. For example, if it’s still under review, the circle is pretty limited, but once an attorney is appointed or a request is denied or sent back, more parties may need to be informed.

context_question: When a request is under review, approved, denied, or sent back, what determines exactly which notices get sent to the defendant, the appointed attorney, jail staff, prosecutor, or other justice partners, and what should happen if someone should not receive a notice in a particular case?
answer: The decision should be driven by the request status, the case type, custody status, and the recipient’s role in that specific case. For example, approval would trigger notice to the appointed attorney and usually the defendant, while a send-back or denial might notify the requesting court and possibly the defendant, depending on the situation. If someone should not receive a notice, the system needs a business rule or suppression flag so that recipient is excluded without breaking the rest of the notifications.

context_question: What conditions should trigger notice suppression for an excluded recipient, and should that suppression be based on a specific case-by-case rule, a recipient-role rule, or a manual flag applied when the notice is generated?
answer: It should be based mostly on case-by-case rules tied to the case type, custody status, and any confidentiality or safety restrictions on that request. A role-based rule makes sense for the default behavior, but we’d still need the ability to override it manually when there’s something unusual about a particular case. Ideally the system would support both, with the manual flag used only when staff need to stop a notice from going out in a specific situation.

context_question: When a request reaches the point of attorney assignment, what specific information or conditions must be present before staff can approve it, and which missing or questionable items should send it to review instead of allowing the appointment to go forward?
answer:
Before approval, we’d need enough verified information to confirm the defendant identity, the correct case, the court making the request, and that the person appears eligible for appointed counsel. We’d also want the request to be complete enough that staff can assign an attorney without having to guess about the charge, location, or any special handling notes.
If something is missing or doesn’t line up, it should go to review instead of moving forward. That would include conflicting identity information, incomplete indigency details, unclear custody status, or any case information that doesn’t match what we have from the court or jail.

context_question: Before a request can move from review to approval, what kinds of legal, operational, or service-delivery constraints should staff take into account when deciding whether it can proceed, and how do those constraints affect the way the request is handled?
answer:
Staff should look at whether the defendant is actually eligible under the court’s rules, whether there are any conflicts or assignment restrictions for attorneys, and whether the case needs a special appointment process because of the charge, court, or custody situation. They also need to consider operational constraints like workload, availability, and whether the request is complete enough to support a defensible appointment.
Those constraints affect how the request is handled by either allowing approval, sending it back for more information, or holding it for review by a supervisor or designated staff. If there’s a legal or policy issue, it shouldn’t just be forced through; it needs to stay in review until the issue is resolved.

context_question: Are there any county technology or procurement constraints—such as approved systems, vendor limitations, licensing, or purchasing rules—that affect how this appointment process must be handled?
answer: Yes, there are usually county-side constraints around approved systems, vendor access, and what can be purchased or integrated, but I don’t know the exact list without checking with procurement and IT. In practice, that can affect whether a notification service, attorney directory, or document exchange has to use an approved platform or a contracted vendor. It may also limit how quickly we can add new interfaces or send data outside county-controlled systems.

context_question: What rules determine which attorney gets assigned to a request, and are there any priority, rotation, conflict, or reassignment rules staff must follow when making that selection?
answer:
Attorney assignment is usually driven by the court, the case type, and the eligible attorney pool for that type of work. In general, staff follow rotation or workload balancing rules, but they also have to check for conflicts, qualifications, language ability, and any special court assignment requirements.
If the first attorney can’t take the case, the request should move to the next eligible attorney or back to review depending on why it failed. Reassignment would need to respect the same conflict and eligibility rules so we don’t accidentally assign someone who shouldn’t be on the case.

context_question: What minimum intake fields must be present before staff can evaluate an appointed-counsel request, and are there any required differences for special case types, missing information, or emergency filings?
answer:
At a minimum, we need the defendant’s identity, the case or cause number, the court, the charge or case type, custody status, and some contact or location information so the request can actually be acted on. We also need whatever indigency or appointment details the court requires, because without that staff can’t really evaluate the request properly.
Yes, special case types can require extra fields, like juvenile, jail-based, or conflict cases, and emergency filings may need a faster path even if the full packet isn’t complete yet. If information is missing, the system should let staff mark it as incomplete and either hold it for follow-up or route it to review, depending on how critical the missing item is.

context_question: When staff mark a request as incomplete, what status options or follow-up states do they need to choose from, and what determines which one they use?
answer:
They’d need at least a way to distinguish between waiting on information, returned for correction, and closed without action if it turns out the request can’t proceed. In practice, the choice depends on whether the missing item can be supplied, whether the request came from the wrong source, or whether there’s a policy or eligibility issue that prevents appointment altogether.
If it’s just missing paperwork or a bad field, I’d expect it to go to a pending-follow-up state. If it’s fundamentally not usable, then returned or closed makes more sense.

context_question: Under what circumstances should a request be treated as an emergency filing rather than following the normal appointment workflow?
answer:
We’d treat it as an emergency when there’s an immediate need for counsel that can’t wait for the normal review cycle, like a same-day hearing, urgent jail matter, or another time-sensitive court action. It also applies when delay would materially affect the defendant’s rights or the court’s ability to move the case forward.
In those cases, the request should bypass the usual queue as much as possible and get routed to staff or a designated reviewer right away. We’d still want enough minimum information to identify the defendant and the case, even if the rest of the intake is filled in afterward.

context_question: What specific county procurement or IT approval requirements should we account for before connecting to outside systems, such as notification services, attorney directories, or document exchange, and are there any data-sharing or vendor-access limits that would block or slow an interface?
answer:
I don’t know the exact county approval steps without checking with IT and procurement, but typically we’d need an approved vendor, a security review, and confirmation that the system can meet county data-handling standards before any connection is built. For interfaces like notifications or document exchange, there may also be contract, licensing, and access-control requirements that determine whether the vendor can receive data directly or only through a county-controlled pathway.
Data-sharing limits could definitely slow things down if we’re sending protected case information, especially if the outside system is not already authorized for justice data. If there are restrictions on external access, that might mean we can only expose limited fields, use batch transfers, or keep the process manual until approval is in place.

context_question: When an attorney is being assigned, what practical rules determine who gets the case next, and how should staff handle conflicts, lack of qualification, or workload issues that prevent the next attorney in rotation from taking it?
answer:
The practical rule is usually to start with the next attorney in the approved rotation or pool for that court and case type, as long as they’re eligible and available. If there’s a conflict, they’re not qualified, or their workload is too high, staff should skip that attorney and move to the next eligible one rather than forcing the assignment.
If no one in the normal sequence can take it, it should go to a supervisor or reviewer for manual assignment. We’d also want the system to record why each attorney was bypassed so there’s a clear audit trail.

context_question: Are there any additional required fields that vary by request category, such as juvenile, jail-based, conflict, or other special case types, that staff must collect before the appointment can be processed?
answer:
Yes, there are usually category-specific fields, but I’d want to confirm the exact list with the courts and the attorney appointments team. Juvenile matters, jail-based requests, and conflict cases often need extra details beyond the basic defendant and case information, such as the facility, detention status, parent or guardian information, or the reason the conflict exists.
For other special case types, there may be court-specific identifiers or appointment restrictions that have to be captured before processing. If those fields aren’t present, the request should probably stay incomplete until the missing category-specific information is provided.

context_question: For those special request types, what specific fields or restrictions must staff verify before a request can move forward, and how should incomplete requests be handled when that information is missing?
answer:
For juvenile requests, staff usually need to verify the child’s identifying information, the parent or guardian contact if available, and the correct court or proceeding. For jail-based requests, the detention location, booking or inmate information, and custody status are key, and for conflict cases we need the reason for the conflict and enough detail to avoid assigning the wrong attorney.
If any of that is missing, I’d expect the request to stay incomplete and not move into appointment until it’s corrected or confirmed. In a few urgent situations we might still allow a temporary review, but we wouldn’t want a final assignment made without the required information.

context_question: What training or guidance should new Office of Attorney Appointments staff receive so they can learn the process quickly and handle routine requests correctly on their own?
answer:
They should get training on the end-to-end intake and appointment workflow, including what information is required, how to spot incomplete or emergency requests, and how to verify eligibility and conflicts. They also need practical guidance on using the system itself, especially how to route requests, document decisions, and handle exceptions without losing the audit trail.
For routine requests, I’d want them to learn with examples from common case types and a clear checklist of when they can process something independently versus when they need a supervisor. A short reference guide or job aid would help a lot so they don’t have to rely on memory for every request.

context_question: What should a new-staff job aid include for handling appointment decisions and exceptions in real time—for example, what boundary conditions, escalation triggers, or documentation steps should it spell out so staff know when they can act on their own versus when they must pause and involve a supervisor?
answer:
It should spell out the basic decision boundaries first, like what counts as a complete request, what fields are mandatory for each request type, and which attorney pools or rotations can be used for that case. Then it should clearly list the situations that stop normal processing, such as a conflict, missing required information, an emergency filing, a questionable eligibility issue, or an attorney who is unavailable or over workload limits.
It should also say exactly what to document before escalating, like who reviewed it, what was missing or unusual, what action was taken, and why the case was paused. If the staff member can’t verify the appointment under the normal rules, the job aid should tell them to stop and send it to a supervisor rather than guessing.

context_question: When staff are documenting a case before escalation, what level of detail should they capture for the review history, the missing or unusual issue, the action taken, and the reason the case was paused so a supervisor can pick it up without having to rework the file?
answer:
We’d want enough detail that a supervisor can understand the situation without reopening the whole intake, so a short but complete summary is ideal. That means capturing who reviewed it, the date and time, the specific missing or unusual issue, what rule or step caused the pause, and what action was already taken, like whether the case was held, routed, or sent back for correction.
If there was any contact with a court, jail, attorney, or other office, that should be noted too, along with any deadlines or urgency. The goal is to make the next reviewer able to pick it up and decide quickly without having to reconstruct the history from scratch.

context_question: When a request is moving through the process, what specific conditions or boundary cases should determine whether it is still handled the same way every time versus paused, rerouted, or escalated so that the appointment remains timely, fair, and consistent?
answer:
It should stay on the standard path when the request is complete, the case type is clear, the defendant and court details match, and the next attorney in rotation is eligible and available. It should be paused, rerouted, or escalated when anything breaks that normal flow, like missing information, a conflict, an attorney not meeting the qualification for that court or case type, workload limits being reached, or a special case that needs supervisory review.
Anything time-sensitive, like a detention matter or a court deadline, should still be handled quickly, but not by skipping the review rules if the assignment would be improper. The main boundary is whether the staff can make the appointment confidently under the standard rules; if not, it needs an exception path with documentation and review.

context_question: Do you want to capture that expectation now as a confirmed requirement for timely, fair, and consistent appointment processing, or should we leave it undecided for the moment?
answer: Yes, I’d capture that now as a confirmed requirement. Timely, fair, and consistent processing is central to what the Office of Attorney Appointments needs, and it should be treated as a baseline expectation for the workflow.

context_question: For an emergency filing, what specific operational criteria should staff use to decide that the request must bypass the normal queue and be routed immediately, and are there any minimum information requirements or exceptions that still have to be met before that happens?
answer:
An emergency filing should bypass the normal queue when there’s a same-day court deadline, an in-custody defendant who needs immediate counsel, or some other time-sensitive situation where waiting would harm the case or the person’s rights. Even then, staff should still need the minimum identifying information, the court or event the request is tied to, and enough detail to understand why it’s an emergency.
I wouldn’t want a bypass to happen with no basic case information at all. If the request is missing something critical, it can be treated as urgent and escalated right away, but it still needs enough information to route correctly and document why it was handled outside the normal process.

context_question: When staff have to pause or escalate an appointment request because they cannot verify it under the normal rules, what exactly should they record about who reviewed it, what was missing or unusual, what action they took, and the reason for pausing it?
answer:
They should record the reviewer’s name or ID, the date and time, and a short note showing what they checked before stopping. They should also capture the exact missing or unusual condition, the action taken, such as held for supervisor review, routed to another queue, or returned for correction, and the specific reason it could not be verified under normal rules.
If there was any deadline, emergency, or outside contact involved, that should be included too. The idea is to leave a clear handoff so the supervisor can see the issue and decide what to do next without starting from zero.

context_question: When staff are deciding whether a request is complete enough to process, what exact minimum information and attorney-pool or rotation rules should they use to determine that they can make the appointment themselves versus needing to stop and send it to a supervisor?
answer:
Staff should be able to process it themselves when they have the defendant’s identifying information, the case number or court information, the charge or case type, and enough data to match the request to the correct appointment pool. They also need to confirm that the next attorney in the rotation is eligible for that court and case type, not conflicted, and not blocked by workload or other assignment limits.
If any of those pieces are missing or if the rotation rules don’t clearly point to an eligible attorney, they should stop and escalate rather than make a guess. That’s especially true when the request crosses into a special appointment category or anything outside the normal pool rules.

context_question: Roughly how many appointment requests do staff need to handle on a typical day, and how many can come in at the same time during those busy court-docket, post-weekend, or holiday periods?
answer:
On a typical day, I’d say it’s probably in the dozens, not just a handful, but not so many that it’s overwhelming every day. During busy docket periods or right after a weekend or holiday, it can stack up quickly and several requests can come in at once, enough that staff need to triage them by urgency and court deadline.
I don’t have an exact count I’m comfortable giving yet, because that would need to be verified with the team. But the system should definitely be able to handle bursts without slowing down the urgent cases.

context_question: For any outside system that would exchange justice or personal data with the county, what specific vendor approval, security review, and data-handling conditions must be met before the interface can go live, and are there any limits on what data can be shared or whether the connection has to stay county-controlled?
answer:
Before any outside interface goes live, it should go through the county’s normal vendor approval and security review process, including whatever legal, IT security, and privacy checks the county requires. I’d expect the interface to be approved only if the vendor is authorized, the data exchange is documented, and there’s a clear agreement on how the data will be protected, logged, and retained.
There should also be limits on sharing only the minimum data needed for the appointment process, and anything sensitive should stay under county control wherever possible. I’d want the connection to remain county-controlled unless the county explicitly approves a different arrangement, because we’re dealing with justice and personal information.

context_question: As you think about moving from the current appointment practices and records to a new approach, what are the main business situations, goals, and operational boundaries we need to understand so the transition works without disrupting day-to-day appointment work?
answer:
The big goal is to move to a system that improves appointment handling without interrupting court operations or slowing down counsel assignment. We need to understand the current queues, the emergency and exception paths, how appointments are approved today, and which records have to be preserved so staff can keep working during the transition.
The main boundary is that day-to-day appointment work can’t stop while we migrate, so we’d need a phased cutover or some kind of parallel support until everyone is confident the new process is stable. We also need to be careful about preserving audit history and not changing the rules for who gets appointed unless the county has formally approved those changes.

context_question: When this interface needs to pull case, defendant, or appointment information from county or justice-community sources, what specific data elements should be shared and what should be kept out of the exchange?
answer:
We should share only what’s needed to identify the person and the case, match the request, and make the appointment, so things like defendant identifiers, case number, court, charge or offense type, filing or setting dates, and current appointment status. If the request needs appointment history or conflict checking, then just the minimum attorney and prior-assignment details required for that purpose.
What should stay out are unnecessary personal details, internal notes that don’t affect the appointment, and anything unrelated to the indigent defense workflow. I’d also want to avoid broad data pulls when a narrower lookup will do, because the exchange should be limited to the minimum necessary data.

context_question: When you’re ready to move from the current process to the new one, what specific operating conditions or approval points should determine whether you use phased cutover, parallel support, or a full switch?
answer:
A phased cutover makes sense if the new process has to be introduced court by court, office by office, or by appointment type because there’s too much risk to switch everything at once. Parallel support is better if staff need time to compare the new results against the current process and make sure appointments, notices, and audit trails all line up before relying on it fully.
A full switch would only be appropriate once the county has signed off that the new workflow is stable, the required data is migrated, and the staff are trained enough to operate without the old process. If there are still unresolved mapping issues, open cases, or heavy exception handling, I’d avoid a full switch.

context_question: When the new process is being rolled out, what practical rules should govern how audit history is kept complete and accessible during the transition, especially if a case or appointment has to move between the old and new workflows?
answer:
The main rule is that the audit trail has to follow the case no matter which workflow it sits in, so nothing gets lost when a record moves from old to new or back again. Staff should still be able to see who requested the appointment, who approved it, when it changed hands, and what system or workflow step handled it.
If a record has to cross between workflows, we should keep a clear cross-reference so the old history and the new history can be tied together without ambiguity. I’d also want the audit information to stay searchable during the transition, because if staff can’t find it quickly, it isn’t really usable.

context_question: How long do you expect the parallel run to last before staff should rely on the new workflow alone, and what condition should tell you it’s safe to end it?
answer:
I’d expect the parallel run to last long enough to cover at least a few normal docket cycles and one or two busy periods, so staff can see how it behaves under real workload. I can’t give you a firm number yet, because that would depend on how quickly the county is comfortable with the results.
It should end when the new workflow is consistently producing the same or better appointment outcomes as the current process, with no major missed notices, data issues, or unresolved exceptions. At that point, staff should be confident they can rely on it without having to check the old process every time.

context_question: During the parallel or phased transition, what practical rules should govern who can see, copy, or transfer sensitive case and personal information, and under what conditions would access need to be limited, masked, or separately approved?
answer:
Only the people who need the information to do the appointment work or verify the record should be able to see it, and copying or transferring it should be limited to approved channels inside the county environment. If the data includes sensitive personal details, juvenile-related information, sealed material, or anything with a special court restriction, access should be narrowed further and may need separate approval.
Masking would make sense for users who only need to confirm identity or case linkage, not the full details. And if a transfer is outside the normal approved workflow or involves a non-county party, I’d expect it to be explicitly reviewed and authorized first.

context_question: When those appointments need information from county or justice-community systems, what practical rules should govern which external sources can be queried, what data can be pulled into the appointment record, and how access should be limited if the source includes sealed, juvenile, or otherwise restricted information?
answer:
Only the systems that are officially part of the indigent defense workflow should be queried, and each query should be tied to a specific case or appointment need rather than broad searching. We should only pull back the data elements needed to complete the appointment, verify the defendant, or support conflict checking, not the full case file.
If the source contains sealed, juvenile, or otherwise restricted information, the system should either block that content from coming through or limit it to users with the proper authority and a documented reason to view it. In practice, I’d want the default to be minimal access, with tighter controls and approvals only when the law or the court rules require it.

context_question: Which specific external systems should be considered officially in scope for indigent-defense appointment work, and are there any case types, appointment stages, or user roles where querying them should be further restricted or disallowed?
answer:
I don’t know the full official list yet, and I’d want to verify that with the county and the justice-community partners before naming systems. In general, anything in the case management, jail, court, prosecutor, and attorney appointment ecosystem could be in scope if it supports the appointment process.
Even then, I’d expect tighter limits for sealed matters, juvenile cases, and any stage where the user doesn’t need the data to complete the appointment. Some roles should probably only see a subset of the information, and some queries may need to be blocked entirely if they go beyond what that role is authorized to do.

context_question: After launch, who should own day-to-day maintenance and issue resolution for the appointment solution, and under what conditions would that ownership shift between the county, the vendor, or justice-community partners?
answer:
Day-to-day ownership should sit with the county, probably through the Office of Attorney Appointments or whichever IT support group they designate, because they’re the ones running the process every day. The vendor should handle defects, configuration support, and upgrades for anything inside the solution itself, while justice-community partners would mainly own corrections to the data or services they provide.
That ownership would shift only when the issue sits outside the county’s control, like a partner system outage, a data feed problem, or a question that requires a vendor fix versus a business process fix. For anything in the gray area, I’d expect the county to coordinate the handoff so staff always know who is responsible and nothing gets dropped.

context_question: What must-have capabilities need to be included in the first delivery of the appointment solution?
answer:
The first delivery has to support receiving appointment requests, reviewing the case and defendant information, assigning or routing the appointment, and sending the needed notifications to the involved parties. It also needs basic audit history, search, and status tracking so staff can see what happened and where each request stands.
I’d also consider integration with the key county and justice-community systems as a must-have if that information is needed to make the appointment decision. Anything beyond that, like more advanced reporting or workflow refinements, could probably wait if it doesn’t affect the core appointment process.

context_question: When an appointment request comes in, what are the key checks or conditions staff must apply to decide whether to assign it immediately, route it elsewhere, or hold it for more information?
answer:
Staff need to confirm the request is complete enough to identify the person, the case, and the type of appointment needed, and then check for any obvious conflicts or restrictions. If the case details are clear and the appointment authority is straightforward, it can be assigned right away.
If something is missing, inconsistent, or the matter belongs to a different court, office, or appointment path, it should be routed or held until the missing information is resolved. I’d also expect any sealed, juvenile, or special-restriction issue to trigger extra review before anyone moves forward.

context_question: When staff are ready to process a request, what should happen if the appointed attorney needs to be changed later because of a conflict, withdrawal, reassignment, or another case change?
answer:
The system should let staff replace the attorney without losing the original appointment history, so there’s a clear record of who was assigned, when, and why it changed. It should also capture the reason for the change, update the current active appointment, and notify the affected parties so everyone has the same information.
If the change is due to a conflict or withdrawal, I’d expect the old appointment to be closed out cleanly before the new one becomes active. That way the audit trail stays intact and there’s no confusion about who represented the defendant at each point.

context_question: When your system needs to pull information from county or justice-community sources, what should happen operationally if one of those sources is unavailable or returns incomplete data at the moment staff are trying to process an appointment?
answer:
If a source is down or comes back incomplete, the appointment should not fail silently. Staff should see a clear message that the data is unavailable or partial, and the request should either be held for follow-up or allowed to proceed only if policy says the missing piece is not essential.
I’d also want the system to keep a record of what was attempted and what came back, so staff can retry later without redoing the whole request. If it’s a critical source, there should be some kind of escalation or alert to the county support team right away.

context_question: When an appointed attorney has to be replaced, what situations or approval rules determine whether the original appointment can be amended in place versus needing the old appointment closed out first and a new one created?
answer:
If it’s just a correction or a straightforward substitution with no break in representation, I’d expect the appointment to be amended in place. That works when the case, court, and assignment basis stay the same and the system can preserve the original history while updating the active attorney.
If the original attorney is formally withdrawing, there’s a conflict, or the case circumstances have materially changed, then the old appointment should be closed out first and a new one created. I’d also expect any approval rules to follow whatever the court or county policy says for that appointment type, especially if a judge or supervisor has to sign off before the change becomes effective.

context_question: When a critical county or justice-community source is unavailable or returns incomplete data, what should the staff workflow be at that moment: hold the appointment, let it continue with a warning, or escalate immediately based on the missing information’s importance?
answer:
It should depend on how important the missing information is to the appointment decision. If it’s critical, staff should be blocked from completing the appointment and it should be held and escalated right away; if it’s helpful but not essential, they should be allowed to continue with a visible warning and a note that the data was incomplete.
In either case, the workflow should make it very clear what happened and what still needs to be resolved. I’d want the system to preserve the partial work so staff can finish it later without starting over.

context_question: When county staff are trying to resolve an appointment issue, what kinds of problems should they handle themselves versus escalating to the vendor or a justice-community partner, and what rule should guide that handoff when the responsibility is not obvious?
answer:
Staff should handle routine corrections, missing case details, simple routing mistakes, and normal appointment updates if they have the information and authority to do it. Anything involving a system outage, integration failure, data mismatch they can’t verify, or an issue owned by another agency should go to the vendor or the justice-community partner.
If responsibility isn’t obvious, the handoff should go to the party that controls the source of truth for the data or process. I’d expect the system to support that with a clear escalation path and a notes trail so the next group knows why it was routed there.

context_question: When a replacement attorney change needs approval, what specific conditions determine whether a judge, supervisor, or other authority must sign off before the change can take effect?
answer:
It should depend on the type of case, the stage of the case, and the reason for the replacement. If the change affects a court-appointed assignment, involves withdrawal for cause, or there’s any policy requirement tied to a specific court or judge, then judicial approval would likely be needed before it takes effect.
For more routine administrative substitutions, a supervisor or appointments staff approval may be enough if county policy allows it. I don’t know the exact authority matrix yet, so that part would need to be confirmed against local rules and appointment policies.

context_question: When an appointment issue could affect timeliness or correctness, what rule should determine whether staff can proceed with the best information available or must stop and escalate before making the change?
answer:
The rule should be based on whether the missing or uncertain information could change the legal correctness of the appointment. If it could affect the defendant’s rights, the appointed attorney’s authority, or compliance with court policy, staff should stop and escalate before changing anything.
If it’s a noncritical detail and the appointment can still be completed accurately enough under policy, they should be allowed to proceed with the best available information and flag it for review. I’d want the system to make that distinction very explicit so staff aren’t guessing in the moment.

context_question: What rules should determine which appointment requests or case details must be protected from broader staff visibility or notifications, and how should the system handle those sensitive items when a request is being reviewed or routed?
answer:
Sensitive items should be restricted based on role, case type, and any legal or court-imposed confidentiality rules. For example, if a detail involves sealed information, juvenile matters, protected witness information, or something the court says should only be seen by specific people, it should not be broadly visible or included in general notifications.
When a request is reviewed or routed, the system should only expose the minimum necessary information to each person involved. If something sensitive has to be flagged for action, I’d want it masked or summarized so the workflow can continue without disclosing the underlying detail to users who don’t have clearance.
